findings.headline: General reserve being drawn down by £0.147m, reducing buffer to £2.288m
findings.detail: The opening reserve balance of £2.435m is forecast to reduce to £2.288m after a £0.147m contribution to the revenue budget (£0.145m budgeted plus £0.002m forecast overspend). The reserve, while adequate, remains modest relative to the £53m+ annual budget.
findings.matters: Ongoing reserve drawdown reduces financial resilience and flexibility to absorb future pressures or opportunities.
findings.figures: Opening balance £2.435m; budgeted contribution £0.145m; Q1 forecast overspend £0.002m; forecast closing balance £2.288m
findings.quote: The forecast closing balance includes the forecast overspend at Quarter 1 of £0.002m, therefore forecasting a balance on the reserve of £2.288m at the end of the financial year

findings.headline: Central Resourcing facing capacity pressures with additional staff costs now included
findings.detail: Central Resourcing is forecasting pressures across its budget with additional staff costs included to reflect capacity constraints. The service is overspending by £0.043m (forecast £0.920m against budget of £0.877m) to address capacity issues as the LCCA grows.
findings.matters: Growing staffing pressures suggest the organization is stretched to manage its expanding remit, which affects delivery risk and operational resilience.
findings.figures: £0.043m overspend in Central Resourcing; forecast outturn £0.920m against budget £0.877m
findings.quote: This service is forecasting pressures across the budget, with additional staff costs included to reflect capacity pressures as the LCCA grows and evolves

findings.headline: Skills and Employment Hub transfer delayed to April 2027 from originally planned August 2026
findings.detail: The Adult Skills Fund was scheduled to transfer to LCCA on 1 August 2026, but the full Skills and Employment Hub transfer is now proposed for 1 April 2027 to ensure complete and safe transfer of all staff and contracts such as Connect to Work. This results in a £3.223m budget reduction for 2026/27.
findings.matters: A major service transfer is being deferred by nine months, affecting the timing of economic development delivery and the LCCA's ability to exercise its full remit.
findings.figures: £3.223m budget reduction; original transfer August 2026, revised transfer April 2027
findings.quote: it is proposed that the Skills and Employment Hub will transfer in its entirety from Lancashire County Council to the LCCA on 1 April 2027, subject to the necessary consultations, as opposed to an in-year transfer as originally budgeted

findings.headline: Fair Pay Agreements implementation contingency of £3m has been released early, suggesting confidence in April 2028 timing or risk appetite on deferral
findings.detail: A £3m contingency created in anticipation of Adult Social Care Fair Pay Agreement costs has been released as part of an underspend, with implementation scheduled for April 2028. The release suggests either high confidence the implementation will not slip into 2026/27, or the council is willing to take the risk of under-providing for potential cost impacts.
findings.matters: Fair Pay Agreements are a known future cost that would materially impact adult social care budgets. Releasing contingency early with an April 2028 implementation date 19 months away suggests either the council expects no slippage (optimistic) or is managing liquidity by releasing reserves now. Either way, it removes a buffer for the 2027/28 year.
findings.figures: £3.0m released from Fair Pay Agreement contingency; implementation scheduled April 2028
findings.quote: release of (£3.000m) from a contingency created in anticipation of financial pressures arising from implementation of Adult Social Care Fair Pay Agreements. Implementation is scheduled for April 2028 and there are no material costs expected in this financial year.

findings.headline: Integrated Care Board discontinuation of Complex Care funding has shifted £2.3m cost burden to the council with no mitigation identified
findings.detail: During 2025/26, the Integrated Care Board discontinued the Complex Care funding stream and applied only National Framework criteria with limited exceptions. This change significantly reduced eligibility for joint funding and shifted £2.3m of cost for children with disabilities to the council. This is recorded as under-delivery of joint funding savings, with no identified compensating savings to offset it.
findings.matters: This represents a transfer of financial risk from the health system to the council with no mitigation. It suggests partnership funding arrangements are becoming less reliable and councils should not assume joint funding contribution levels will be maintained. The 'significantly reduced eligibility' language suggests this change was not negotiated but imposed.
findings.figures: £2.3m arising from Integrated Care Board decision to discontinue Complex Care funding stream; described as 'significantly reduced eligibility for joint funding arrangements'
findings.quote: the forecast overspends relating to placements and family support services for children with disabilities include £2.3m arising from the under-delivery of joint funding savings following the Integrated Care Board's decision during 2025/26 to discontinue the Complex Care funding stream and apply only the National Framework criteria, with limited exceptions. This change has significantly reduced eligibility for joint funding arrangements and consequently increased financial pressures on the Directorate.

findings.headline: Waste Management is highly exposed to international commodity markets and disposal costs, creating forecast volatility despite planned £7m recurring savings
findings.detail: Waste Management forecasts £2.4m overspend despite having plans to deliver £7m recurring annual savings. The current overspend (£0.9m from waste sector volatility and £1.5m from procurement/implementation delays) reflects exposure to international markets and unpredictable disposal costs. Proposed mitigation includes capital investment in ANPR CCTV at recycling centres and shredding equipment to reduce disposal costs, but these require capital funding and procurement completion.
findings.matters: Waste is exposed to external commodity and disposal markets. Even with operational improvements planned, the council faces ongoing exposure to cost volatility. The reliance on capital investment to realise savings means cost pressure may persist until capital projects complete.
findings.figures: Waste Management £2.4m forecast overspend (£0.9m from market volatility, balance from savings lag); £7m recurring savings planned; sector 'highly volatile and exposed to international markets'
findings.quote: The waste sector is however highly volatile and exposed to international markets (such as fuel) and unpredictable disposal costs. This does make forecasting challenging and is currently impacting the service budget by £0.900m.

findings.headline: Property rationalisation programme is not delivering planned Facilities Management savings due to limited market conditions for income and tenancies
findings.detail: Facilities Management forecasts £2.2m overspend, with delays in property rationalisation programme being a key driver. The council is actively trying to secure additional tenants at County Hall and expand external utilisation of The Exchange conferencing facility. However, market conditions are limiting opportunities, preventing achievement of planned savings in 2026/27 and 'potentially beyond'. Also experiencing forecast increases in gas and electricity costs.
findings.matters: Property rationalisation is a common council strategy for releasing capital value and reducing operating costs. If market conditions for commercial lettings are weak enough to prevent the council achieving planned savings, this suggests either the property estate is not well-positioned for income generation or the commercial market is softer than assumed. The 'potentially beyond' caveat suggests uncertainty about forward recovery.
findings.figures: Facilities Management £2.202m overspend; property rationalisation programme showing market-driven delays
findings.quote: Whilst this continues to be actively explored, market conditions are limiting the opportunities available which has impacted the achievement of planned savings in 2026/27 and potentially beyond.

findings.headline: Place directorate savings programme is slipping by £6m into next year, with external cost pressures adding £2m unbudgeted spend
findings.detail: Place directorate forecasts £8.6m overspend (4.86% of budget). Of this, £6m reflects delayed savings delivery expected now in 2027/28 instead of 2026/27. Separately, fuel and utility cost volatility tied to Iran conflict is adding £2m unbudgeted pressure: energy costs for street lighting expected to rise 8% from October, highways fuel costs up £0.4m, Facilities Management also facing gas/electricity increases.
findings.matters: Savings slippage indicates delivery governance may not be robust — the council describes these as timing differences but they are still pressuring the current year position. External cost pressures tied to geopolitical risk (Iran conflict) suggest the council faces ongoing exposure to international commodity price volatility beyond its control.
findings.figures: Place £8.568m total overspend; £6m savings delays; £2m fuel/utility pressure; Highways energy cost increase 8% from October (£0.3m); fuel costs £0.4m; Waste Management £2.4m forecast overspend; Procurement £1.1m contract savings shortfall
findings.quote: Firstly, continued volatility in fuel and utility markets, linked to the impact of the conflict involving Iran, is expected to result in additional cost pressures of approximately £2.0m during the financial year. Secondly, delays in the delivery of approved savings are forecast to contribute a further £6.0m of overspend.

findings.headline: Children in care numbers and placement mix are shifting toward more expensive residential provision despite Family Safeguarding programme
findings.detail: Children in care increased from 1,680 (April 2025) to 1,766 (June 2026). More significantly, residential placements have shifted from 190 children in children's homes (August 2020) to 284 (June 2026). This change in placement mix, combined with higher unit costs, is driving £10.5m overspend in Children's Social Care placements. Where Our Children Live programme (in-house provision) has implementation delays due to property works and Ofsted registration, slowing the pace of cost avoidance.
findings.matters: Residential care is substantially more expensive than other placements. The shift toward residential, combined with rising numbers, suggests either the council's Family Safeguarding model is not reducing demand as planned, or the complexity of cases is increasing. Delays in in-house residential delivery mean cost pressures will persist longer than originally forecast.
findings.figures: Children in care: 1,766 (June 2026) vs 1,680 (April 2025); residential placements 284 vs 190 in August 2020; total CSC placement overspend £10.5m; CwD placement overspend £2.1m; also £2.3m shortfall from Integrated Care Board discontinuing Complex Care funding stream
findings.quote: the number of CIOC increased to 1,766 in June 2026. Whilst overall numbers remain below historic levels, the profile of placements has changed, with the number of children placed in children's homes increasing from 190 in August 2020 to 284 in June 2026. This shift in placement mix, together with higher average weekly costs, reflects increasing levels of complexity and need.

findings.headline: Adult social care overspend of £7.1m at Q1 driven by unbudgeted demand and rising care costs despite planned fee uplifts
findings.detail: Older People and Physical Disability (OPPD) services alone forecast £8.6m overspend with 12,150 people supported against 11,860 budgeted. Unit costs rising from £610 to £625/week (+2.6%) despite planned 5.5% fee uplifts, suggesting care market cost pressure is outpacing the council's ability to manage it. Learning Disabilities and Mental Health both show similar pattern: more people needing care at higher unit costs than anticipated.
findings.matters: Adult social care is the largest council spend and demand-led. Structural overshooting of both volume and unit costs suggests either planning assumptions are outdated or cost pressures in the care market are beyond council control. Both indicate ongoing pressure on revenue rather than one-off variance.
findings.figures: OPPD £8.579m overspend; 12,150 people vs 11,860 budgeted; unit costs £625/week vs £610 budgeted (+2.6%); Learning Disabilities £2.305m overspend with 3,824 people (up 24 from prior year); Mental Health £1.923m overspend with 1,645 people (up 48 from prior year); total Adults £7.109m overspend
findings.quote: OPPD Services are forecasting an overspend of £8.579m, representing the most significant financial pressure within Adults Services. As at the end of Quarter 1, 12,150 people were being supported at a total gross weekly cost of £7.599m against a relevant weekly budget of £7.420m for 11,860 people.

findings.headline: SEND funding structural mismatch persists: deficit forecast to reach £424.55m by March 2028 without government intervention
findings.detail: The Council's SEND reform plan projects the DSG deficit would grow to £424.55m by March 2028 absent the High Needs Stability Grant. This reflects a long-standing structural funding gap where DSG allocations have not kept pace with rising SEND demand.
findings.matters: This is not a temporary variance but a structural problem that signals unsustainable education pressures. Even with government grant support, the deficit remains material and will grow again from 2027/28 onwards, suggesting the council faces years of education funding pressure.
findings.figures: DSG deficit forecast £424.55m by March 2028 without High Needs Stability Grant; £187.27m by March 2028 with grant
findings.quote: Due to the increasing demand, the Council's SEND reform plan shows that the DSG deficit is forecast to grow to £424.55m by March 2028.

findings.headline: Government grant support conditional on DfE approval of SEND reform plan; approval status not yet confirmed
findings.detail: The £91.44m High Needs Stability Grant (covering 90% of the DSG deficit) is contingent on the council's SEND reform plan being approved by the Department for Education. The plan was submitted 19 June 2026, but DfE approval is not guaranteed and the paper provides no approval date.
findings.matters: The council's financial position relies on external government approval of a reform plan. Rejection or significant delay would eliminate the £91.44m grant, leaving the full £253.48m deficit to be funded from general reserves or force deeper service cuts.
findings.figures: High Needs Stability Grant £91.44m (covering 90% of deficit); deficit reduction dependent on approval: £253.48m to £162.04m
findings.quote: Due to the increasing DSG deficits forecasted nationally, the government has recently announced the High Needs Stability Grant, which subject to the approval of the Council's SEND reform plan from the Department for Education (DfE), will cover 90% of the DSG deficit at March 2026, estimated at £91.44m

findings.headline: In-year DSG deficit doubled from January forecast: Q1 monitoring identified additional £75.98m pressure
findings.detail: The January 2026 budget report forecast a DSG shortfall of £75.90m. By Q1 (30 June 2026), an additional £75.98m budget pressure had been identified, doubling the forecast deficit to £151.88m in just six months.
findings.matters: A 100% increase in forecast deficit within one quarter suggests either weak forecasting or rapidly deteriorating demand that is difficult to predict and control, increasing uncertainty around the council's financial position.
findings.figures: January forecast shortfall £75.90m; Q1 additional pressure £75.98m; total 2026/27 in-year pressure £151.88m
findings.quote: At Quarter 1 monitoring an additional £75.98m budget pressure is forecast, totalling a forecast in-year budget pressure of £151.88m.

findings.headline: Accumulated DSG deficit forecast at £253.48m, remaining at £162.04m by March 2027 even with conditional government grant
findings.detail: The 2025/26 deficit of £101.60m plus the 2026/27 in-year deficit of £151.88m creates an accumulated deficit of £253.48m. The High Needs Stability Grant (£91.44m) would reduce this only to £162.04m if approved. The deficit is then forecast to grow again to £187.27m by March 2028.
findings.matters: A growing accumulated DSG deficit indicates the council's revenue base cannot sustain education spending under current funding arrangements. This structural deficit must be funded from general reserves or service cuts, weakening the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: 2025/26 deficit £101.60m; 2026/27 in-year pressure £151.88m; accumulated total £253.48m reducing to £162.04m (with grant), then £187.27m by March 2028
findings.quote: With the deficit brought forward from 2025/26 of £101.60m, the accumulated DSG deficit is forecast at £253.48m.

findings.headline: High Needs Block overspending by £149.87m (65.8%) due to growing SEND demand and placement costs
findings.detail: The High Needs Block budget of £227.84m is forecast to reach £377.71m. The largest pressures are commissioned services (£42.98m overspend), mainstream school placements (£25.20m), and alternative provision (£3.19m). The council states that DSG funding has not increased in line with growing SEND demand over many years.
findings.matters: DSG deficits must be covered from the council's general fund, creating direct pressure on other services and affecting borrowing capacity. A £149.87m overspend in one block represents material financial risk to lenders assessing council creditworthiness.
findings.figures: High Needs Block budget £227.84m vs forecast £377.71m; Commissioned Services £42.98m overspend; Mainstream Schools £25.20m
findings.quote: The most significant variance relates to the High Needs Block with an overspend of £149.87m forecast due to the growing demand and placement costs for pupils with Special Educational Needs & Disabilities (SEND).

findings.headline: Council pursuing 'invest to save' capital schemes to relieve revenue budget pressures
findings.detail: The document notes that invest-to-save opportunities are being reviewed by services to relieve revenue pressures, and future capital requests will need careful prioritization against remaining headroom. This indicates the council is considering using capital investment to offset revenue budget strain, a common signal of underlying revenue tightness.
findings.matters: When councils turn to invest-to-save schemes to manage revenue pressures, it can signal tight revenue budgets. Lenders monitor whether such schemes deliver the promised savings or create additional debt service costs on revenue budgets already under strain.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this paper
findings.quote: Invest to save opportunities are being looked at by services to relieve revenue pressures; it needs to be considered how these are deemed a priority in comparison to the rest of the capital programme.

findings.headline: Q1 capital spending forecast at 97% of revised budget with notable delays in highways (bridges) and schools delivery
findings.detail: The Q1 forecast shows £262.944m will be spent against the revised budget of £271.116m, an underspend of £8.173m (3.01%). The shortfall is attributed to delays in the highways bridges programme due to resource and operational constraints, and schools projects deferred to next financial year. The council notes this early-year position involves high levels of assumptions with regular monitoring planned throughout the year.
findings.matters: A 3% underspend at Q1 could signal delivery risk or cash constraints, particularly when delays are tied to resource constraints rather than seasonal factors. If this tracks as a full-year underspend, it affects the council's capital deployment capabilities.
findings.figures: Forecast spend £262.944m vs revised budget £271.116m; variance (£8.173m) or 3.01%. Highways underspend (£2.072m), Schools High Need Provision underspend (£2.920m), Schools Condition underspend (£2.922m)
findings.quote: The forecasted spend for 2026/27 as at Quarter 1 is £262.944m, giving a variance against the capital programme budget of (£8.173m), c3.01%.

findings.headline: Total capital programme reduced 7.2% (£21m) with revised plan still interim pending final Efficiency Review conclusions in November 2026
findings.detail: The overall approved capital programme has been cut from £292.162m to £271.116m. Critically, the document explicitly states this is an interim position pending completion of Phase 2 of the Efficiency Review, which is not due to be finalised until November 2026. This means further material changes to the capital plan are expected within the financial year.
findings.matters: An interim 7.2% cut with more changes pending creates uncertainty for lenders assessing the council's capital deployment and borrowing needs. November changes midway through the year could trigger further revisions and signal underlying strategic uncertainty.
findings.figures: Capital programme reduced from £292.162m to £271.116m (£21.046m reduction, 7.2%)
findings.quote: In addition, for 2026/27, the capital programme was identified as an area of review for Phase 2 of the Efficiency Review, with the early work (due to be finalised by November 2026) reflected in the updated delivery programme of £271.116m. This is an interim position, pending completion of the Efficiency Review work.

findings.headline: Schools Basic Need capital spending cut 77% (£39.4m to £9m) due to SEND reform and reconsideration of high needs plans
findings.detail: The most dramatic reallocation in the revised programme sees Schools Basic Need spending collapse from £39.368m to £9.000m, while Schools High Need Provision increases from £11.177m to £13.918m. The council explicitly links this shift to SEND reform requiring reconsideration of high needs provision, suggesting a material rebalancing of schools capital away from expansionary basic need toward special educational needs capacity.
findings.matters: This represents both a service priority shift and potential exposure to national SEND funding pressures which have destabilised many council budgets. A lender would want to understand whether this is sustainable or a precursor to revenue pressure from SEND commitments.
findings.figures: Basic Need from £39.368m to £9.000m (£30.368m reduction, 77%); High Need Provision from £11.177m to £13.918m (£2.741m increase)
findings.quote: Schools – variances are forecast across the schools condition and high needs block due to some school projects being delayed to next financial year, and the SEND reform resulting in a consideration of upcoming high needs plans.

findings.headline: Borrowing approved capital spend reduced from £53.4m to £37.7m through Efficiency Review focusing on Property, Waste and Digital Services
findings.detail: The revised capital programme reflects a significant reduction in borrowing across the council. Originally approved borrowing of £53.401m has been cut to £37.711m through Phase 2 of the council's Efficiency Review, which has specifically targeted borrowing-funded areas to reduce debt service costs. This represents a £13.690m reduction in planned new borrowing.
findings.matters: A 26% cut to approved capital borrowing signals either heightened focus on debt management, constrained borrowing headroom, or a reassessment of capital priorities. Lenders need to understand whether this reflects prudent deleveraging or reaction to tighter debt capacity.
findings.figures: Borrowing reduced from £53.401m to £37.711m (£13.690m reduction, 25.6%)
findings.quote: The Efficiency Review focussed on areas of borrowing to seek to secure reduced borrowing costs which impacts on areas such as Property, Waste and Digital Service.

findings.headline: Adults and Children's social care combining for £11.087m overspend, reflecting SEND and adult placement demand outpacing budgets
findings.detail: Adults, Health & Wellbeing faces £7.109m overspend (1.27%) with pressures in commissioned services, whilst Children's Social Care faces £3.978m overspend primarily from placements and family support for children with disabilities. These pressures mirror the SEND demand spike in the DSG High Needs Block, indicating demand is unmet across multiple budget lines.
findings.matters: Unmet social care demand across both adult and children's services, aligned with SEND pressures, indicates a structural underfunding that will not resolve without additional resources. This creates ongoing cost pressures across multiple budget years.
findings.figures: Adults £7.109m overspend (1.27%), Children's Social Care £3.978m overspend, combined £11.087m
findings.quote: Adults, Health and Wellbeing Services – A total overspend of £7.109m (1.27%) is forecast, with pressures across commissioned services. The projected outturn reflects several risks, including an expectation that further savings will be achieved in the remainder of the financial year. Children's Social Care – An overspend of £3.978m is forecast for Children's Social Care primarily on placements and family support for children with disabilities

findings.headline: Place Directorate showing 4.86% overspend (£8.568m), the worst performance of any service area, with waste disposal costs rising £0.9m and property savings delayed
findings.detail: Place (waste, highways, property, economic development) is forecasting a £8.568m overspend, the largest variance by percentage. Waste alone is £2.4m over, driven by £1.5m delayed savings on the Farington anaerobic digestion facility and £0.9m in rising transport and processing costs. Facilities Management faces £2.2m overspend from delayed property rationalisation savings.
findings.matters: The oversized Place variance and cascading delays across multiple projects (waste facility, property disposal) indicate delivery capacity constraints within the council's capital and revenue programmes.
findings.figures: Place Directorate £8.568m overspend (4.86% of £176.5m budget), Waste Management £2.4m over (£1.5m delayed savings), Facilities Management £2.2m over
findings.quote: Place 176.459 185.027 8.568 4.86% ... an overspend of £2.4m is projected which relates to a combination of delayed delivery of savings of £1.5m (although mitigation plans are underway to avoid this recurring in 2027/28) and £0.9m cost increases at household waste recycling centres relating to increased transport costs and the cost of processing recycled waste.

findings.headline: SEND High Needs Block overspend of £149.87m with accumulated deficit reaching £253.48m even after government grant approval
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block faces an in-year overspend of £149.87m due to placement costs for pupils with SEND outpacing funding growth. The accumulated deficit (including £101.60m brought forward) will reach £253.48m even if the recently announced High Needs Stability Grant (covering 90% of the 2025/26 deficit) is approved by DfE. The Council must fund 10% of the deficit itself, and faces material borrowing costs to service the growing deficit whilst the statutory override remains in place.
findings.matters: This is a structural funding gap that persists even with government support. The 10% council-funded portion and unfunded future deficits create a liability that will require either budget reductions elsewhere or sustained borrowing, both of which constrain financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £151.88m in-year DSG overspend (9.7%), High Needs Block £149.87m, accumulated deficit £253.48m with grant, council must fund 10% of deficit plus borrowing costs
findings.quote: The 2026/27 Dedicated Schools Grant Revenue Position shows a forecast in-year budget pressure of £151.88m (9.7%) ... Whilst the DSG deficit is currently covered by the statutory override, there will still be a cash flow impact as the deficit increases, meaning an increased need to borrow.

findings.headline: Revenue overspend of £15.655m in Q1 with savings delivery at only 87%, signalling control weaknesses early in year
findings.detail: The Council is already £15.655m (1.18%) overspent at end of Q1. More significantly, the £73.9m savings programme is forecast to deliver only 87% (£64.555m), creating a £9.345m gap. Place Directorate faces a £6m shortfall against its £18m savings target, with service delays in waste, highways and property pushing realisation to 2027/28.
findings.matters: An early-year overspend combined with savings underdelivery indicates the council is already struggling to manage its budget. Early-year delays in Place suggest delivery challenges may persist into 2027/28, creating an ongoing structural problem.
findings.figures: £15.655m Q1 overspend, £9.345m savings shortfall (13% of £73.9m target), Place Directorate £6m shortfall against £18m target
findings.quote: The total forecast revenue outturn position for 2026/27 at the end of Quarter 1 is an overspend of £15.655m, which represents 1.18% of the approved budget ... Current forecasts indicate a £6m shortfall in 2026/27 across Waste Management, Highways, Property and Procurement.

findings.headline: Integrated Care Board decision to discontinue Complex Care funding stream created £2.3m unplanned pressure on Children with Disabilities services.
findings.detail: During 2025/26, the ICB decided to discontinue the Complex Care funding stream and apply only National Framework criteria. This decision 'significantly reduced eligibility for joint funding arrangements'. The CwD directorate is reporting £2.3m of placement overspend arising from under-delivery of joint funding savings caused by this external partner decision, a figure not forecast when the budget was approved.
findings.matters: This is an external organisation's policy decision creating material, unbudgeted cost for the council. It highlights dependency on partner bodies for funding and the risk when those arrangements change without adequate notice or alternative funding.
findings.figures: £2.3m pressure arising from ICB funding decision impact on joint funding savings shortfall. CwD total overspend includes £2.1m placement costs.
findings.quote: This change has significantly reduced eligibility for joint funding arrangements and consequently increased financial pressures on the Directorate... £2.3m arising from the under-delivery of joint funding savings following the Integrated Care Board's decision during 2025/26 to discontinue the Complex Care funding stream and apply only the National Framework criteria, with limited exceptions.

findings.headline: External cost shocks from fuel and utility market volatility linked to Iran conflict are creating £2.0m additional uncontrollable cost pressure in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The Place Directorate is forecasting £2.0m additional cost from fuel and utility price volatility. Specifically, energy costs for street lighting are forecast to increase 8% from October 2026 (£0.300m pressure), fuel costs for highways maintenance creating a £0.400m pressure, and Facilities Management also facing gas/electricity increases. The council has limited ability to mitigate these external price pressures.
findings.matters: Geopolitical factors are directly impacting council finances. These costs are largely uncontrollable and reveal the council's exposure to commodity price volatility. If conflict persists or energy prices remain elevated, the pressure may extend beyond one financial year.
findings.figures: Total fuel/utility pressure approximately £2.0m. Street lighting energy up 8% from October 2026 (£0.300m). Highways fuel £0.400m. Waste management exposed to international fuel markets.
findings.quote: continued volatility in fuel and utility markets, linked to the impact of the conflict involving Iran, is expected to result in additional cost pressures of approximately £2.0m during the financial year.

findings.headline: Place Directorate is forecasting £6.0m delay in delivering approved savings, with council assuming these move to 2027/28, concentrating savings realization risk into next year.
findings.detail: Place is reporting £6.0m of forecast overspend directly attributed to 'delays in the delivery of approved savings'. The council notes these are expected to be delivered in 2027/28, 'reflecting timing differences in implementation rather than a permanent non-delivery'. However, multiple service areas show similar slippage: Highways £0.700m, Facilities Management (property rationalisation delays), Procurement £1.1m shortfall. Finance and Commerce also reports 'challenges in delivering planned savings'. The pattern suggests over-optimistic savings planning or capability constraints.
findings.matters: If these delays reflect capability or external constraints rather than purely timing, it increases risk that 2027/28 will face a compressed savings delivery programme with higher failure risk. Q1 position is already constrained; if savings do not recover, the council will face structural deficit.
findings.figures: Place delayed savings £6.0m. Place total overspend £8.568m (4.86% of budget). Procurement savings shortfall £1.1m (though service has delivered £8m+ since 2023/24). Highways maintenance £0.700m delayed.
findings.quote: delays in the delivery of approved savings are forecast to contribute a further £6.0m of overspend. However, the majority of these savings remain achievable and are currently expected to be delivered in 2027/28, meaning the forecast reflects timing differences in implementation rather than a permanent non-delivery of savings.

findings.headline: Children's services placement costs are rising with residential provision up 50% since 2020, while the WOCL programme designed to manage costs faces implementation delays.
findings.detail: The number of children in residential placements has increased from 190 in August 2020 to 284 in June 2026. CSC placement overspend is £10.5m. The Where Our Children Live (WOCL) programme, intended to reduce reliance on external residential placements through in-house capacity, is experiencing delays. The council states: 'implementation timescales have, in some cases, been longer than originally anticipated due to factors including property-related works and Ofsted registration requirements.' Delays are affecting the pace of savings realisation.
findings.matters: The shift to higher-complexity, higher-cost residential placements is continuing. The programme intended to mitigate this through in-house capacity has slipped, pushing cost management into future years. This creates risk if either demand continues to rise or planned capacity does not materialise.
findings.figures: Residential placements: 190 (Aug 2020) to 284 (June 2026). CSC placement overspend £10.5m. CIOC (Children in Our Care) increased from 1,680 (April 2025) to 1,766 (June 2026). CwD residential placements: 31 (2024/25 average) to 36 (June 2026).
findings.quote: the number of children placed in children's homes increasing from 190 in August 2020 to 284 in June 2026. This shift in placement mix, together with higher average weekly costs, reflects increasing levels of complexity and need and continues to place pressure on budgets due to the substantially higher unit cost of residential provision.

findings.headline: Adult social care services forecasting £7.109m overspend (1.27%) at Q1 2026/27, driven primarily by OPPD Services.
findings.detail: OPPD (Older People and Physical Disability) Services are forecasting £8.579m overspend. At Q1, the council is supporting 12,150 people against budget for 11,860 - an additional 310 people. Learning Disabilities and Autism (£2.305m overspend) and Mental Health (£1.923m overspend) are also reporting demand pressures. The council is managing unit costs (increasing 2.6-3.4% against planned uplifts of 3.65-5.5%) but absolute volumes exceed forecast.
findings.matters: This is structural overspend in a core statutory service. Rising demand is continuing into 2026/27 despite mitigation efforts. Cost management is working but cannot offset higher volumes of people requiring care.
findings.figures: OPPD £8.579m overspend; 12,150 people supported vs 11,860 budgeted (310 more); weekly cost £7.599m actual vs £7.420m budget; unit costs £610→£625 per person per week (2.6% increase). Learning Disabilities £2.305m overspend; Mental Health £1.923m overspend.
findings.quote: OPPD Services are forecasting an overspend of £8.579m, representing the most significant financial pressure within Adults Services. As at the end of Quarter 1, 12,150 people were being supported at a total gross weekly cost of £7.599m against a relevant weekly budget of £7.420m for 11,860 people.

findings.headline: School capital programmes being deferred; £30m cut to Basic Need and SEND reform creating further planning uncertainty
findings.detail: Schools Basic Need cut from £39.368m to £9m; additional deferrals across condition and high needs. Document notes SEND reform is 'resulting in a consideration of upcoming high needs plans', suggesting the reform creates uncertainty about future school provision requirements.
findings.matters: Significant deferral of school capital indicates constraints on service expansion; SEND reform uncertainty may create further volatility in school capital needs and budgets.
findings.figures: Schools Basic Need £39.368m → £9m (-£30.368m); Schools Condition variance -£2.922m; High Needs variance -£2.920m
findings.quote: Schools – variances are forecast across the schools condition and high needs block due to some school projects being delayed to next financial year, and the SEND reform resulting in a consideration of upcoming high needs plans.

findings.headline: Highways programme delayed due to resource and operational constraints despite £15m additional investment
findings.detail: Despite adding £15m to highways (described as an Administration priority), Q1 forecast shows £2.072m underspend with bridges schemes delayed. The cause is stated as 'resource and operational constraints', not funding limitations.
findings.matters: Inability to deploy increased capital allocation due to operational constraints suggests management and delivery capacity issues beyond finance; this raises questions about the council's ability to execute capital programmes.
findings.figures: £15m additional highways investment; £2.072m Q1 variance forecast
findings.quote: Highways - a variance of (£2.072m) is forecast which predominantly relates to the bridges programme, where some schemes are expected to be delivered later than originally planned due to resource and operational constraints.

findings.headline: Capital programme remains interim with further material changes expected from Efficiency Review Phase 2 by November 2026
findings.detail: The £271.116m revised programme (down £21m from February approval) is explicitly marked interim, pending completion of Phase 2 work due November 2026. This means further changes are expected mid-year.
findings.matters: A 7.2% mid-year reduction plus signalled further changes create planning uncertainty and suggest original budget assumptions are not holding; additional cuts are likely.
findings.quote: This is an interim position, pending completion of the Efficiency Review work.

findings.headline: Revenue budget pressures driving consideration of capital investment to solve revenue shortfalls
findings.detail: The document explicitly states that services are examining 'invest to save' capital schemes to relieve revenue pressures, and that these will need to be weighed against other capital priorities. This indicates the revenue budget is under strain and the council is considering capital investment as a solution to revenue problems.
findings.matters: Using capital investment to solve revenue shortfalls is a risky practice; it suggests structural revenue budget difficulties that cannot be solved through normal means.
findings.figures: None quantified
findings.quote: Invest to save opportunities are being looked at by services to relieve revenue pressures; it needs to be considered how these are deemed a priority in comparison to the rest of the capital programme.

findings.headline: Capital programme reduced from £292.162m to £271.116m pending completion of Efficiency Review
findings.detail: The capital programme was cut by £21.046m (7.2%) between February 2026 and now. The report states this is an interim position pending completion of Phase 2 of the Efficiency Review, due in November 2026. This suggests further reductions or reprofilings may follow.
findings.matters: A 7% cut to the capital programme mid-year indicates either slippage or a reassessment of the council's capital priorities and delivery capacity. Further cuts may follow once the efficiency review completes
findings.figures: Original programme £292.162m, revised programme £271.116m, variance £21.046m (7.2%)
findings.quote: The 2026/27 Capital Programme agreed by Full Council in February 2026 was £292.162m… This has resulted in an updated delivery programme of £271.116m. This is an interim position, pending completion of the Efficiency Review work.

findings.headline: Waste management hit by both delayed savings delivery and transport/processing cost inflation
findings.detail: Waste is overspending by £2.4m: £1.5m from delayed delivery of savings (mitigations underway for 2027/28) and £0.9m from cost inflation at recycling centres due to transport and processing costs. This shows both execution risk on savings and external price pressures.
findings.matters: Two independent adverse movements hitting the same budget simultaneously suggests neither was anticipated. The delayed savings indicate the original plan was optimistic; the cost inflation shows exposure to market prices the council cannot fully control
findings.figures: Total overspend £2.4m: delayed savings £1.5m, cost inflation £0.9m
findings.quote: Waste Management – an overspend of £2.4m is projected which relates to a combination of delayed delivery of savings of £1.5m (although mitigation plans are underway to avoid this recurring in 2027/28) and £0.9m cost increases at household waste recycling centres relating to increased transport costs and the cost of processing recycled waste.

findings.headline: Adults, Health and Wellbeing overspend of £7.109m driven by commissioned services pressures
findings.detail: The council's largest single service area is forecast to overspend by £7.109m (1.27% of its £560.702m budget). The overspend reflects pressures across commissioned services, though the council expects further savings to be achieved by year-end.
findings.matters: At £7.1m this is the largest single directorate overspend. Adult social care is structurally challenged nationally; this overspend suggests the council's budget assumptions for commissioned care prices or volumes were insufficient
findings.figures: £7.109m overspend on £560.702m budget (1.27%)
findings.quote: Adults, Health and Wellbeing Services – A total overspend of £7.109m (1.27%) is forecast, with pressures across commissioned services.

findings.headline: High Needs Stability Grant covers only 90% of 2025/26 deficit and remains subject to DfE approval
findings.detail: The government announced a High Needs Stability Grant that would cover 90% of the DSG deficit at March 2026 (estimated £91.44m), leaving the council with 10% (£10.16m) as its own cost. Receipt is contingent on DfE approval of the council's SEND reform plan, submitted 19 June 2026, with feedback awaited.
findings.matters: The relief is partial, conditional, and not yet approved. If the DfE rejects or delays the reform plan, the council faces the full £253m liability immediately. Even with approval, £162m remains on the books
findings.figures: High Needs Stability Grant estimated at £91.44m (90% of 2025/26 deficit); accumulated deficit after grant £162.04m
findings.quote: Due to the increasing DSG deficits forecasted nationally, the government has recently announced the High Needs Stability Grant, which subject to the approval of the Council's SEND reform plan from the Department for Education (DfE), will cover 90% of the DSG deficit at March 2026, estimated at £91.44m.

findings.headline: SEND demand growing faster than DSG funding allocation has increased for many years
findings.detail: The council states that SEND placement costs and numbers are rising materially, but DSG funding has not kept pace for years. This creates a structural mismatch between funded growth and actual demand growth in special education.
findings.matters: If demand is genuinely structural (not cyclical), and funding is not following, the deficit will continue to widen year on year. This suggests the statutory override will eventually have to cover an ongoing service cost, not just catch-up from a one-time spike
findings.figures: High Needs Block: £149.87m overspend on £227.84m budget
findings.quote: Consistent with many councils nationally, the DSG funding allocation for many years has not increased in line with the growing demand. The Council continues to face significant challenges with the increasing numbers of pupils with SEND, bringing significant financial and service pressures in this context.

findings.headline: Schools DSG deficit forecast to accumulate to £253.48m, with borrowing required once statutory override ends
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant (High Needs Block for SEND) is forecast to overspend by £151.88m in 2026/27 alone. Combined with the £101.60m deficit brought forward from 2025/26, the accumulated deficit reaches £253.48m. Currently covered by statutory override, but this creates a cash-flow impact requiring the council to borrow against a future liability.
findings.matters: A £253m accumulated deficit is a structural liab­ility that will require borrowing once the override is lifted. A lender needs to understand whether this is a temporary grant-funded issue or if the council faces a permanent funding gap in SEND
findings.figures: In-year overspend £151.88m (9.7%), brought forward deficit £101.60m, accumulated deficit £253.48m; High Needs Block overspend £149.87m on budget of £227.84m
findings.quote: The Schools Budget (Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG)) at Quarter 1 is forecast to overspend by £151.880m (9.7%) due to the growing demand and placement costs for pupils with Special Educational Needs & Disabilities (SEND). Whilst the DSG deficit is currently covered by the statutory override, there will still be a cash flow impact as the deficit increases, meaning an increased need to borrow.

findings.headline: Place Directorate faces £6m shortfall in £18m savings programme, mostly from implementation delays pushed to 2027/28
findings.detail: Place Directorate (Waste, Highways, Property, Procurement) was required to deliver £18m of savings. Current forecasts show only £12.811m will be delivered in 2026/27, a shortfall of £5.656m. The council states most of this variance is attributable to implementation delays, with savings expected in 2027/28.
findings.matters: A third of one directorate's entire savings plan is not delivering. While delays can be recovered, they push revenue pressure into next year and test whether the council can execute under pressure
findings.figures: £18m required savings, £12.811m forecast, £5.656m shortfall; Place Directorate net budget £176.459m, forecast £185.027m (£8.568m overspend, 4.86%)
findings.quote: The most significant challenge in delivering the Council's savings programme lies within the Place Directorate, which is responsible for achieving £18m of savings. Current forecasts indicate a £6m shortfall in 2026/27 across Waste Management, Highways, Property and Procurement. However, the majority of this variance is attributable to implementation delays, with the associated savings now expected to be realised in 2027/28.

findings.headline: Revenue overspend of £15.655m at quarter one with only 87% of planned savings on track
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £15.655m overspend (1.18% of approved budget) at the end of Q1. Of the £73.9m in agreed savings, only £64.555m is forecast to be delivered, a shortfall of £9.345m. Services are implementing mitigation strategies to address this, but effectiveness will only be seen at Q2.
findings.matters: A material overspend in the first quarter combined with only 87% savings delivery creates a compound problem: the council has both an immediate shortfall and a structural savings gap it may not close
findings.figures: £15.655m overspend (1.18%), £73.9m planned savings, £64.555m forecast delivery (87%), £9.345m shortfall
findings.quote: The total forecast revenue outturn position for 2026/27 at the end of Quarter 1 is an overspend of £15.655m, which represents 1.18% of the approved budget. The 2026/27 budget contains agreed savings of £73.9m with delivery currently forecast to be 87%

findings.headline: Council's DSG deficit position is conditional on DfE approval of SEND reform plan to unlock £91.44m High Needs Stability Grant
findings.detail: The council submitted its SEND reform plan to the Department for Education on 19 June 2026. Government has announced the High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of the DSG deficit (estimated £91.44m at March 2026). With grant approval, the 2027 deficit reduces to £162.04m; without it, the full £253.48m deficit remains. By 2028, even with grant support, the deficit grows to £187.27m.
findings.matters: The council's financial position depends on external government approval for a reform plan; failure or delay in DfE approval would leave the full deficit unsupported and materially worsen the financial position.
findings.figures: £91.44m grant (90% of deficit), submitted 19 June 2026, £162.04m 2027 position with grant, £187.27m 2028 position with grant
findings.quote: the government has recently announced the High Needs Stability Grant, which subject to the approval of the Council's SEND reform plan from the Department for Education (DfE), will cover 90% of the DSG deficit at March 2026, estimated at £91.44m

findings.headline: High Needs Block overspend of £149.87m driven by growing SEND demand and placement costs that have outpaced funding allocations for years
findings.detail: SEND-related expenditure is the primary driver of the DSG crisis. Mainstream schools placements show a £25.20m overspend, and commissioned services (including SEND support) show £42.98m overspend. The council explicitly states funding allocation has not kept pace with demand growth.
findings.matters: This reveals a structural, long-term funding gap where service demand is growing faster than central allocation—a problem that cannot be resolved through efficiency alone and requires either reform or sustained additional funding.
findings.figures: £149.87m High Needs Block overspend, £25.20m mainstream schools, £42.98m commissioned services, £2.19m special schools
findings.quote: the DSG funding allocation for many years has not increased in line with the growing demand. We continue to face major challenges with the increasing numbers of pupils with SEND, bringing significant financial and service pressures

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant forecast to be £151.88m in deficit for 2026/27, increasing the accumulated deficit to £253.48m
findings.detail: The DSG was set with a forecast shortfall of £75.90m but Q1 monitoring reveals an additional £75.98m budget pressure. The accumulated deficit brought forward from 2025/26 is £101.60m, taking the total projected deficit to £253.48m. Forecast to grow further to £424.55m by March 2028 if current demand trends continue.
findings.matters: A quarter-billion pound deficit significantly constrains the council's financial flexibility and borrowing capacity; it signals systemic pressure in children's services funding nationally.
findings.figures: £151.88m in-year pressure (9.7% of DSG budget), £75.90m original forecast shortfall, £75.98m additional, £253.48m accumulated deficit, £424.55m projected by March 2028
findings.quote: the accumulated DSG deficit is forecast at £253.48m. Due to the increasing demand, the Council's SEND reform plan shows that the DSG deficit is forecast to grow to £424.55m by March 2028.

findings.headline: Both Liberal Democrat and Labour amendments propose eliminating Preston bus gate enforcement fines, which would cost the council £1.5m annually in lost revenue.
findings.detail: Liberal Democrat amendment proposes a 2-year trial removal of bus gate fines for Preston Corporation Street and New Hall Lane, estimated at £1.5m reduced income. Labour amendment makes an identical proposal to remove bus gate fines on a trial basis at the same cost. The financial implications tables show this as revenue foregone, though amendments identify RSG and contingency to cover the loss.
findings.matters: For a lender, voluntary revenue reductions indicate the council may choose to forgo income streams, affecting financial resilience. The fact that two separate political groups have proposed identical revenue losses suggests political will to eliminate this funding source.
findings.figures: £1.5m annual income loss
findings.quote: For a period of 2 years scrap the Preston Corporation Street Bus Gate plus New Hall Lane which will result in estimated reduced income of £1.5m.

findings.headline: Multiple amendments propose significant prudential borrowing for capital schemes, potentially totalling £25m+ across highways, Community Safety, and school infrastructure.
findings.detail: Progressive amendment proposes £5m prudential borrowing for Community Safety and highways schemes. Liberal Democrat amendment proposes £8m additional borrowing for enhanced road repairs, pavements, and traffic infrastructure. Labour amendment proposes £12.5m prudential borrowing in each of 2027/28 and 2028/29 for new school capital. Each amendment includes revenue budget provision for borrowing costs.
findings.matters: For a lender, accumulated prudential borrowing increases the council's debt service obligations and reduces future borrowing capacity. The cumulative effect across multiple schemes could materially affect the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £5m (Progressive), £8m (LD), £12.5m per year (Labour)
findings.quote: To provide a fund of £5m for Community Safety and related highways schemes funded by prudential borrowing; the borrowing costs to be funded from RSG and revenue savings.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Investment Decisions 2025-26 Final Report
findings.headline: High-priority action: Council must complete strategic review of investment losses and their impact by 31 March 2026
findings.detail: The audit identifies as a high-priority (urgent) action that management must review the impact of the £200m investment losses and their effect on the council in the medium to short term. Management must also review the Treasury Management Strategy itself to set appropriate limits on the length and value of individual investments. Additionally, the council is required to seek specialist advice on market strategies to offset losses and on accounting treatment of losses.
findings.matters: This is not academic—the auditor is flagging that the council's current strategy and delegated authority have enabled commitments that have crystallised major losses. A lender needs to know whether the council has a plan to manage this and whether the strategy will be changed to prevent recurrence.
findings.figures: Target date: 31 March 2026; £200m losses to be reviewed; £548m projected returns if held to maturity
findings.quote: Complete a strategic review of the impact of the losses arising from decisions taken under the Treasury Management Strategy and the impact of the fall in value of the investment in the medium to short term.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Investment Decisions 2025-26 Final Report
findings.headline: Audit commission triggered by elected member scrutiny and multiple Freedom of Information requests, indicating loss of confidence in treasury decision-making
findings.detail: This audit was explicitly commissioned in response to member scrutiny and several FOI requests regarding transparency and accountability of investment decisions. This indicates concern at committee level about the council's treasury management, particularly around the two major long-term investments (EDF bonds and inflation-linked gilts) and their transparency.
findings.matters: When elected members are requesting audits and making FOI requests about investment decisions, it signals they do not have confidence in executive assurance or transparency. This is a warning sign for lenders about governance culture.
findings.figures: Number of FOI requests unspecified; audit scope triggered by member scrutiny
findings.quote: This audit was commissioned by the former interim Director of Finance and Commerce in response to scrutiny from elected members and a number of Freedom of Information requests.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Investment Decisions 2025-26 Final Report
findings.headline: Treasury Management Practices last formally updated in 2012/13 and contain contradictions regarding delegated responsibilities between Director of Finance and Director of Investment
findings.detail: The Treasury Management Practices document is significantly outdated and contains contradictory guidance on whether the Director of Investment has delegated authority or merely presents options to the Director of Finance. While clarified in practice (Director of Investment handles operational decisions, Director of Finance handles strategic decisions), the formal procedures document does not reflect this and has not been formally approved by the Director of Finance.
findings.matters: Outdated, contradictory procedures create risk that officers may misinterpret their authority. This contributes to decisions like the EDF bonds falling outside stated policy—staff working from unclear guidance cannot be expected to maintain compliance.
findings.figures: TMPs last formally documented 2012/13; current version remains under review without formal sign-off
findings.quote: The Treasury Management Practices contained a contradiction regarding delegated responsibilities. While they stated that the Director of Investment was responsible for Treasury Management decisions, they also indicated that the Director should only present options to the Director of Finance.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Investment Decisions 2025-26 Final Report
findings.headline: Critical governance gap: files belonging to the Director of Investments were lost or corrupted during a transition, removing audit trail for investment decisions
findings.detail: The audit was unable to review key decision documentation because files held by the Director of Investments were either lost during a transition or corrupted and could not be recovered. This absence of securely stored, centralised records undermines transparency and governance. The audit notes operational records like forecasts and reconciliations were well maintained, but strategic documentation capturing rationale and approvals was limited or missing.
findings.matters: Loss of decision records is a fundamental governance failure that prevents verification of compliance, due diligence, and decision rationale. It raises questions about whether controls are actually working and whether the council can demonstrate sound decision-making to auditors and lenders.
findings.figures: Director of Investments' files lost or corrupted; formal Treasury Management meeting documentation declined in recent years
findings.quote: The auditor was informed that the Director of Investments' files were either lost during the transitioning process or had been corrupted and were unable to be recovered.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Investment Decisions 2025-26 Final Report
findings.headline: EDF bond investment breached the approved counterparty credit matrix by not holding an AA credit rating
findings.detail: The council invested £ in EDF bonds in 2019 without an AA credit rating as required by the counterparty credit matrix, though this was justified under the separate Non-Treasury Management Investment Strategy 2019-20 based on French government backing (80% ownership at time of investment). The investment was approved by the Director of Finance but was not explicitly mentioned in the Treasury Management Strategy despite being material. The audit confirms compliance with the Non-Treasury Management Strategy, but notes this represents a breach of the main Strategy's counterparty requirements.
findings.matters: This shows a gap between formal policy and execution—a key audit and governance concern for lenders. It indicates either the strategy was not being followed or policy exceptions were being made without explicit documentation, both of which signal control weaknesses.
findings.figures: EDF credit rating outside approved matrix; French government 80% ownership at time of investment; 3.18% semi-annual interest rate
findings.quote: Although EDF's credit rating was not an AA credit rating, and so was outside the approved counterparty matrix, the council's Non-Treasury Management Strategy for 2019–20 allowed for such investments subject to approval by the Director of Finance.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Investment Decisions 2025-26 Final Report
findings.headline: Approximately £200 million in unrealised capital losses on two long-term investments with maturities extending to 2073 and 2114
findings.detail: The council holds UK inflation-linked gilts purchased in 2021 showing a market value loss of £217m (maturity 2073) and EDF bonds purchased in 2019 currently showing a loss of £61m (maturity 2114). While these investments continue to generate annual income (£3.4m and £3.7m respectively), the scale of unrealised losses has created strategic risks and governance challenges. The audit notes these losses would crystallise if the assets were sold, creating an opportunity cost and preventing funds from being used for other investments or council priorities.
findings.matters: Lenders assess a council's financial position and exposure to market volatility; £200m in losses on investments held to maturity represents a material structural challenge and limits financial flexibility. Finance directors need assurance the council has a plan for managing these exposures.
findings.figures: £200m combined unrealised losses; £217m gilt loss; £61m EDF loss; £3.4m annual gilt income; £3.7m annual EDF income; 2073 and 2114 maturity dates
findings.quote: While these investments were intended to provide stable, inflation-protected income and support long-term reserves, market conditions in 2022 led to significant unrealised capital losses of approximately £200 million. These losses would only crystallise if the assets were sold

findings.headline: Budget balance depends on delivery of £62m savings (5% of net budget) with unproven track record
findings.detail: The 2026-27 budget requires £62m in total savings, representing 5% of the council's net budget. These comprise £42.927m of savings agreed in February 2025, £23.256m of additional savings identified in November 2025, and £2.644m of reprofiled savings. While the council notes that the majority of 2025-26 savings were delivered, the current year's £6.2m overspend suggests cost control is difficult.
findings.matters: Large savings targets, especially newly identified ones, carry significant delivery risk. Any slippage would require either further cuts or drawdown of reserves. The council's current budget control problems raise doubts about execution capability.
findings.figures: £62m total savings; 5% of net budget; £42.927m agreed; £23.256m additional
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget is underpinned by the delivery of savings totalling £62m in 2026/27. Any reductions to the delivery programme would mean alternative savings need to be found or support would be required from reserves.

findings.headline: Internal Audit opinion gives only moderate assurance on governance and internal control frameworks
findings.detail: The council's Internal Audit function gave a moderate assurance opinion (not strong assurance) on the adequacy of governance, risk management, and internal control frameworks in its 2024-25 annual report. The Section 151 Officer has concluded that the Internal Audit function's resources are insufficient for the scale and complexity of the council, and the budget increases audit funding by £0.5m annually.
findings.matters: Moderate assurance indicates gaps in the internal control environment. The fact that the CFO considers audit resources inadequate suggests oversight is currently below what should be expected for a £1.3bn organisation.
findings.figures: £0.5m additional annual funding for Internal Audit
findings.quote: The Internal A nnual Report for 2024/25 presented to the Audit, Risk and Governance Committee in July 2025 gave moderate assurance overall on the adequacy of the design and the effectiveness of the Council's frameworks for governance, risk management, and internal control.

findings.headline: Current budget year tracking to £6.2m overspend despite mitigation efforts, following earlier £28m and £10.4m forecast misses
findings.detail: Q3 2025-26 forecast shows a £6.2m overspend expected at outturn. This follows much larger forecast misses earlier in the year: Q1 predicted £28.0m overspend and Q2 predicted £10.4m. Executive Leadership Team has put mitigations in place, but the council continues to forecast an overspend. Primary containment risks are in Adult Social Care and Home to School Transport.
findings.matters: The pattern shows the council has chronic difficulty forecasting and controlling expenditure in its two largest cost areas (ASC and HTST). Even with multiple mitigation rounds, it remains off-track. This undermines confidence in the ability to deliver next year's budget.
findings.figures: Q1 forecast £28.0m overspend; Q2 forecast £10.4m overspend; Q3 forecast £6.2m overspend
findings.quote: an overspend of up to £6.2m may come to hand when outturn is declared for that year

findings.headline: Adult Social Care experiencing structural funding gap between available resources and cost of statutory duties
findings.detail: Demand pressures in Adult Social Care are forecast to grow £14.1m in 2026-27, £29.7m in 2027-28, and £46.8m in 2028-29. Combined with inflation pressures of £26.2m, £47.1m, and £70.4m respectively, the council explicitly acknowledges a widening gap between funding and the real cost of meeting statutory duties. Drivers include ageing population, NHS transfer of discharged patients, workforce shortages, and National Living Wage pressures.
findings.matters: The council has explicitly identified this as a structural (not cyclical) gap, indicating the service is financially unsustainable at current funding levels. This is a medium-term solvency risk and a major cost pressure.
findings.figures: Demand growth 2026-27 £14.068m; inflation 2026-27 £26.213m; combined three-year demand growth £121.6m; combined three-year inflation £143.7m
findings.quote: These combined demographic, NHS and market pressures in the context of requirements for improvement from the CQC Regulator are creating a widening structural gap between available funding and the real cost of meeting statutory duties, placing significant and ongoing pressure on the council's financial resilience and service sustainability.

findings.headline: Special Educational Needs & Disabilities demand growth forcing £29.954m new investment with uncontrolled trajectory
findings.detail: The budget allocates £29.954m for SEND pressures in 2026-27: £7m for Inclusion Services, £17.7m for Home to School Transport demand growth, and £5.254m for borrowing costs related to DSG cash-flow. The paper notes significant backlogs in EHCP assessments, national SEND reform impacts, and workforce shortages affecting both timeliness and quality of service delivery.
findings.matters: SEND is an uncontrolled statutory service. The majority of the cost increase (£17.7m) is for expensive home-to-school transport. This demand is both driving the DSG deficit and consuming increasing General Fund resources with no clear containment strategy.
findings.figures: £29.954m total; £7.000m Inclusion; £17.700m Home to School Transport; £5.254m borrowing
findings.quote: Demand for statutory SEND services remains one of the most acute pressures within the system. Increased requests for Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP) assessments, alongside backlogs arising from national SEND reforms and workforce shortages, have impacted on timeliness and quality.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit forecast to reach £419.90m by 2028-29, growing at accelerating rate with borrowing costs escalating
findings.detail: The council's DSG deficit stands at £95.51m currently. The budget forecasts a £75.90m in-year deficit for 2026-27, growing to £123.38m by 2028-29, resulting in a cumulative deficit of £419.90m by 2028-29. Borrowing costs to cash-flow this deficit are forecast at £11.5m (2026-27), £17.5m (2027-28), and £25.6m (2028-29). The statutory override funding the council currently relies on expires in 2028-29, creating a cliff-edge.
findings.matters: The deficit is growing faster than expected and becomes a material unfunded liability when Government support ends in 2028-29. This creates medium-term solvency risk and indicates the underlying issue (SEND demand) is not being controlled.
findings.figures: Opening balance £95.51m; 2026-27 deficit £75.90m; cumulative 2027-28 £296.52m; cumulative 2028-29 £419.90m; borrowing costs £11.5m, £17.5m, £25.6m
findings.quote: Along with the majority of upper tier councils – the Council has faced the prospect of a growing and unfinanced DSG Deficit. This is a feature of most upper tier councils that have responsibility for Children's and Education services at the present time largely driven by demand for SEND services.

findings.headline: Very Long Term Investment Portfolio of £519m holds £350m unrealised loss, constraining financial flexibility
findings.detail: The council holds £519m in government and commercial bonds with maturities to 92 years, acquired in earlier years. The current yield is no longer competitive with market alternatives, and the bonds have fallen significantly in value. If liquidated now, the council would incur losses around £350m. The council receives £16.9m annual income from these holdings but is managing this as a material financial constraint on its medium-term operations.
findings.matters: This is a major constraint on the council's financial flexibility and borrowing capacity. The existence of this portfolio forces the council to set aside £15-22.5m annually into a new Working Capital Enhancement Reserve to manage the cashflow implications. Any forced realisation could be materially damaging.
findings.figures: £519m invested, £350m unrealised loss, £16.9m annual income, 92-year maturities
findings.quote: the yield from holding these bonds is no longer attractive relative to other yields available in the money markets and accordingly the value of the bonds has fallen. For this reason, if the bonds were sold at the present time the Council would likely incur losses on sale in the region of £ 350m.
